title: Lucid is not significantly closer than MTurk on all five personality traits
published: Formal hypothesis tests demonstrate that Lucid is significantly closer to the ANES 2012 than MTurk on [[all five traits]].
corrected: Formal hypothesis tests demonstrate that Lucid is significantly closer to the ANES 2012 than MTurk on [[four of the five traits, extraversion excepted]].
note: Appendix Table 1 prints 0.100 and 0.052 for extraversion's distance and bootstrapped standard error. Those two numbers give `z` = 1.92 and a two-tailed p-value of 0.054, above the 0.05 threshold; the table's own p-value column prints 0.034, which is the deposit's expression rather than the two-tailed test. The maintained rewrite's seeded run reaches the same conclusion, at `z` = 1.79 and p = 0.074. The other four traits clear 0.05 by a wide margin under either test.

title: The number of significant differences in the online appendix
published: Out of 21 opportunities, Lucid is closer to the ANES 18 times, [[14]] of which are significant.
corrected: Out of 21 opportunities, Lucid is closer to the ANES 18 times, [[13]] of which are significant.
note: Extraversion is the difference between the two counts, for the reason given above. Recomputing every p-value from the distance and standard error appendix Table 1 prints gives the same 13. The sentence that follows it is unaffected: MTurk is closer in 3 instances and significant in one, voter turnout, under both tests.

title: Six demographic differences are significant, not five
published: Out of the 11 demographic variables that are measured for both Lucid and MTurk, the Lucid mean is closer to the ANES mean in nine instances, [[five]] of which are statistically significant.
corrected: Out of the 11 demographic variables that are measured for both Lucid and MTurk, the Lucid mean is closer to the ANES mean in nine instances, [[six]] of which are statistically significant.
note: Appendix Table 1 prints a p-value below 0.05 for Female, Education, Age, Mean income, Black and South, and Lucid is the closer sample on all six. The count is the same under the two-tailed test corrected in the first two entries, so it does not turn on which p-value is used.

title: The MTurk sample under-represents southerners
published: The regional balance on Lucid comes very close to the 2012 ANES, whereas the MTurk sample appears to [[overrepresent]] southerners.
corrected: The regional balance on Lucid comes very close to the 2012 ANES, whereas the MTurk sample appears to [[underrepresent]] southerners.
note: The southern share is 30.1 per cent on MTurk against the ANES 2012 benchmark of 37.2, so MTurk sits 7.1 points below it; Lucid is at 37.6. Figure 1, which is where the sentence sends the reader, plots the same thing in standard deviations: MTurk at –0.146 and Lucid at 0.009, with the benchmark at zero. MTurk over-represents the Northeast and the Midwest instead. Appendix Table 1 is unaffected: it reports the distance between the two samples rather than the direction of either, and its South row is right.

title: The standard errors and p-values of appendix Table 1 are one draw from an unseeded bootstrap
published: Table 1's Bootstrapped SE and p-value columns are [[one draw from a 100-resample bootstrap for which the deposited code sets no seed]]. Neither column is reproducible: running the deposited procedure again moves it, and moves the count of significant differences the appendix states along with it.
corrected: [[This edition prints a 125,000-resample bootstrap at a declared seed]]. All 21 distances are unchanged and reproduce the published column exactly; thirteen of the 21 standard errors and ten of the 21 p-values differ from it at the three decimals the table prints.
note: The sampling error of a bootstrap standard deviation is about `SE / sqrt(2B)`. At the deposit's `B` = 100 that is roughly 0.0035 on a standard error near 0.05, three times the last digit the table prints, which is why `appendix_table_1_bootstrap_stability.R` recovers the published count of 14 significant differences on only 39.5 per cent of 200 seeds, ranging 12 to 15. At `B` = 125,000 it falls to 0.00015, about a seventh of that last digit, and the printed column stops being a property of the seed. Nothing here moves a distance, a sign, or the size of any difference, which is what the appendix's argument rests on. What it does settle is the two counts corrected in entries 1 and 2: at this precision they no longer turn on which of the two p-value expressions is used, because extraversion falls short of 0.05 under both.

title: A missing space in the healthcare rumor study manifest
published: [[Control:(No]] introduction before asking the rumor belief question.)
corrected: [[Control: (No]] introduction before asking the rumor belief question.)
note: The item is in section 2.5.1 of the online appendix. The published page sets no space between the bold `Control:` and the parenthesis after it, where the parallel item in section 2.4.1 sets one and so does every other labelled condition in the manifest. It is the page's own spacing and not an extraction artifact: read off the rendered PDF at 300 dpi, the bold run ends and the roman run begins at the same horizontal position, against a gap of one space width in section 2.4.1. No comparison of text can see it, because a space is not a token.

title: A missing word in the Discussion
published: While we think the theories that underlie most survey experiments conducted in the USA would extend to Lucid, we emphatically do not mean [[to]] that any experiment conducted on a convenience sample is relevant for theory.
corrected: While we think the theories that underlie most survey experiments conducted in the USA would extend to Lucid, we emphatically do not mean [[to imply]] that any experiment conducted on a convenience sample is relevant for theory.
note: The published page sets "do not mean to that", which is ungrammatical: a verb is missing after "to". The authors' own LaTeX source for the article, in the archived working folder, reads the same, so the omission is not the publisher's typesetting. The paragraph around it separates a theory's predictions extending to a sample from that sample being drawn at random from a population, and the sentence is the authors declining the stronger reading of their own argument, so the missing verb is one of "imply", "say" or "suggest". "Imply" is the one supplied here and the choice is recorded rather than presented as a reading of the page: nothing in the paragraph turns on which of the three it is.

title: The p-value column of appendix Table 1 is not the two-tailed test the appendix describes
published: Because no formula for the standard error of this procedure is available, we use the nonparametric bootstrap to estimate sampling variability and we obtain [[two-tailed p-values under a normal approximation]].
note: The sentence sets the method on the same page as the table whose last column it describes, and the column is not that test. The deposited `12_DistanceTests.R` computes `pnorm(2 * (1 - abs(z)))`, so the published column is that expression read at the distance and standard error the table prints, and the preamble gives the cause and the threshold it moves. Against the two-tailed p-value computed from those same two printed numbers, the column's 21 cells read, in the table's order, Female 0.000 against 0.001; Education 0.000 against 0.000; Age 0.000 against 0.000; Mean income 0.000 against 0.003; White 0.873 against 0.661; Black 0.000 against 0.000; Hispanic 0.357 against 0.230; Northeast 0.179 against 0.143; Midwest 0.409 against 0.258; South 0.010 against 0.032; West 0.948 against 0.858; Voter registration 0.157 against 0.129; Voter turnout 0.000 against 0.005; Party ID 0.010 against 0.033; Ideology 0.000 against 0.000; Political Interest 0.000 against 0.000; Extraverted 0.034 against 0.054; Agreeable 0.001 against 0.008; Conscientious 0.000 against 0.000; Stable 0.000 against 0.000; Open 0.005 against 0.023. The two columns disagree about significance at 0.05 for one characteristic, extraversion, which entry 1 corrects in the sentence that counts it, and entry 2 corrects the count that follows from it. No corrected column is set here. Entry 7 already changes how the bootstrap behind the same cells is drawn, so a second correction to them would put two values in one cell, and which statistic the table should report is a choice for the authors and not a token the page supplies. No conclusion of the paper changes: Lucid is closer to the ANES on eighteen of the 21 characteristics under either column, the large differences sit where the paper puts them, and extraversion is the one characteristic the choice of expression moves across the threshold.

title: Two sentences on one page disagree about which sample is closer on voter turnout
published:
Voter registration and turnout seem to vary somewhat across samples, with [[the Lucid sample corresponding more closely to the 2012 ANES baseline for voter registration and voter turnout]].

Lucid is significantly closer to the ANES 2012 on party identification, ideology, and political interest, while [[MTurk is significantly closer for voter turnout]].
note: The two sentences are on one page and disagree about turnout. Each is supported by a file the authors deposited, and the two files carry different ANES 2012 turnout benchmarks. The standardized file the distance tests read puts it at 0.702, which makes MTurk the closer sample and gives appendix Table 1 its distance of -0.124, a two-tailed p-value of 0.005 from the page's own distance and standard error. The political table's weighted mean puts the same benchmark at 0.756, against Lucid's 0.763 and MTurk's 0.706, which makes Lucid the closer sample. Voter registration is unaffected. Correcting either sentence would mean choosing between two deposited benchmarks, which is an analytical decision about what the ANES baseline is and not a token the page supplies, so the edition reprints both as published. No conclusion of the paper changes: Lucid is closer on party identification, ideology, and political interest under either benchmark, and the registration comparison favours Lucid under both.

title: The welfare heterogeneity section names a 2016 GSS the deposit does not hold
published:
We assess whether the treatment effect of receiving the "assistance to the poor" versus "welfare" phrasing varies among white, black, and Latino respondents, among both the Lucid sample and respondents in the [[2016 GSS]].

While the point estimates for the [[2016 GSS]] CATEs are nearly identical, in the Lucid sample white respondents exhibited larger treatment effect magnitude than black or Latino respondents, though again these differences are not statistically significant.
note: The deposited welfare data hold the 1984 and 2014 General Social Surveys and no other, 943 and 2,457 usable respondents, and the article's own Experiment 1 section names the 2014 GSS as the baseline. The deposited `standardizedExperimentsHeterogeneousEffects.RData`, which supplies the original panel of Figure 3, is a pre-computed table whose comparison sample is labelled "Original" with no year and which no deposited script builds, so which of the two surveys the panel draws on cannot be established from the deposit. A corrected sentence would have to name a year this edition cannot verify, so both sentences are reprinted as published. No conclusion of the paper changes: the sentences report low heterogeneity among white, black, and Latino respondents in both samples, a statement about the CATEs and not about the year of the survey that supplies them.
